long.title: Why Did Abraham Refuse a King's Fortune? | The Full Story of the Covenant | Genesis 14-15 (KJV)
long.first_comment: He would not take a shoelace from the king of Sodom, and God said, I am thy reward. What have you had to let go of?

narration.text: That is Abram. A few days earlier he had beaten an army of four kings with three hundred and eighteen men. He had refused a fortune from a king. And now, alone in the dark, he tells God what frightens him most. Not the armies. Something else.
How does a hero end up here? To understand it, we have to go back to the war.
This is the full story of Genesis fourteen and fifteen: a war of kings, a mysterious priest, a fortune refused, and the night God made a covenant under the stars.

Four kings from the east, led by Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, had ruled the cities of the plain for twelve years. In the thirteenth year the cities rebelled. In the fourteenth year the kings came back.
They swept down the whole land like a storm. Town after town, people after people. Giants, mountain tribes, desert peoples. Nobody stood against them.

And there went out the king of Sodom, and the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Admah, and the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (the same is Zoar;) and they joined battle with them in the vale of Siddim;
With Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and with Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five.
And the vale of Siddim was full of slimepits; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and fell there; and they that remained fled to the mountain.
The cities of the plain were left wide open.
And they took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their victuals, and went their way.
And they took Lot, Abram’s brother’s son, who dwelt in Sodom, and his goods, and departed.
Remember the last time we saw Lot. He pitched his tent toward Sodom. Now he lives inside it, and Sodom has just lost its war. Lot is a prisoner of war.
And there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew; for he dwelt in the plain of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner: and these were confederate with Abram.
Abram the Hebrew. This is the first time anyone in the Bible is called a Hebrew. It probably means the one from the other side, the outsider who crossed over.
And when Abram heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued them unto Dan.

Stop and think about the odds. Four kings who had just crushed five kings. And against them, one old shepherd with three hundred and eighteen men from his own household. Nobody would have blamed him for staying home.
From the oaks of Mamre to Dan is well over a hundred miles. On foot, through the hills, chasing an army with days of head start, and every hour Lot was dragged further away.
Abram was not a soldier. He was a shepherd with a household. But the man who once lied to save himself is now running toward danger to save someone else.
And he divided himself against them, he and his servants, by night, and smote them, and pursued them unto Hobah, which is on the left hand of Damascus.
He split his small force and struck at night, from more than one side. In the dark, a few hundred men can sound like an army. By dawn the eastern kings were running north past Damascus.
And he brought back all the goods, and also brought again his brother Lot, and his goods, and the women also, and the people.

Notice what Abram does not say. He does not say, Lot chose Sodom, let Lot live with it. The nephew who took the best land is the one he risks everything to save. That is love that does not keep score.
And the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him, at the valley of Shaveh, which is the king’s dale.
And here the story slows down, because two kings come to meet Abram in the same valley. One of them will bless him. The other will try to buy him.
And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.

Salem is very likely the city later called Jerusalem. Melchizedek appears out of nowhere. No father is named, no mother, no beginning and no end. Centuries later, the Psalms and the letter to the Hebrews will remember this man as a picture of a greater Priest.
And he blessed him, and said, Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth:
And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all.
Abram gives him a tenth of everything, and admits who really won this war. Remember that title. Abram is about to use it.
And the king of Sodom said unto Abram, Give me the persons, and take the goods to thyself.

It sounds generous. Keep the treasure, just give me back my people. But think about who is offering. The king of the very city the Bible calls wicked beyond measure. It is a test, and everyone is watching.
And Abram said to the king of Sodom,
Remember Egypt. There he grew rich from a lie. This time he will not take even a shoelace. Abram has learned something: whoever makes you rich will want to own your story.
He will not let a king of Sodom say that he made Abram great. The only one allowed to make his name great is God, exactly as He promised in Haran.
And then, after the battle, after the blessing, after the refused fortune, comes the night.
After these things the word of the Lord came unto Abram in a vision, saying, Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.
This is the first time the Bible says the word of the Lord came to a man. And the first words are: Fear not.

Fear not. God only says that to someone who is afraid. The man who attacked four kings was afraid. Maybe of revenge from the east. Maybe of a king whose gold he had just refused. Maybe of dying with no son.
I am thy reward. Abram had turned down the king's fortune, and God answers: you did not lose a reward. I am your reward.
And Abram answers with the question you heard at the very beginning, about a servant named Eliezer.

Old contracts from that part of the world show that a childless man could adopt a trusted servant to inherit everything. That was Abram's plan. It was sensible. It was legal. And it was not what God had promised. Abram had stopped expecting more.
And Abram said,
Notice that God does not rebuke him for asking. This is what honest faith sounds like. It is not pretending you have no questions. It is bringing them to God. And God answers him directly.
And, behold, the word of the Lord came unto him, saying, This shall not be thine heir; but he that shall come forth out of thine own bowels shall be thine heir.
And he brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be.
In a sky with no city lights, thousands of stars are visible to the eye. God takes an old man with no son outside and says: start counting. Count them, Abram. If you can.
And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness.

This is one of the most important sentences in the whole Bible. Abram did not do anything here. He believed. And God counted that trust as righteousness. Paul will build whole chapters on this one verse. Before the law, before the temple, before any ritual, a man believed, and God called it right.
Then God speaks again, and Abram, who has just believed, asks for something to hold on to.
And he said unto him, I am the Lord that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it.
Ur: the journey began long before Haran.
And Abram answers with one more question. Faith and questions can live together.
And he said unto him, Take me an heifer of three years old, and a she goat of three years old, and a ram of three years old, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon.
And he took unto him all these, and divided them in the midst, and laid each piece one against another: but the birds divided he not.
Then he waits.
And when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away.

In Abram's world this is how a covenant was made. Two parties walked between the halves and said: if I break my word, let this happen to me. Abram waits all day, guarding the path, for God to come. Some see in the birds everything that tries to steal a promise.
And when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him.
This is no peaceful dream.
And he said unto Abram, Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years;
And also that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge: and afterward shall they come out with great substance.

That is Egypt, and that is the Exodus, four hundred years before it happens. God tells Abram the hard part first. Slavery, then judgement, then freedom. The promise is sure, but it will not be quick. Even the delay is part of the promise.
And thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace; thou shalt be buried in a good old age.
But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.
God is patient even with the Amorites, and He is never late.
And it came to pass, that, when the sun went down, and it was dark,
behold a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp that passed between those pieces.
Fire in the dark, walking alone between the pieces.
Look at who walks between the pieces. Only the fire. Abram is asleep. God takes the whole weight of the promise on Himself, and asks Abram only to trust.
In the same day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates:
Have given. Not will give. God speaks of it as already done, to a man who still has no son and does not own a single field. Every road he walked, inside one promise.
The Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites,
And the Hittites, and the Perizzites, and the Rephaims,
And the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.
Ten peoples lived in that land. Abram owned none of it. In his whole life he would buy only one field, with a cave to bury Sarah in. He died holding a promise, not a deed.
He refused a king's gold, and that same night God said, I am thy reward. Some things you have to let go of before you can hear that.
And notice: the man God counted righteous still asked hard questions, twice in one night. Faith is not silence. It is trusting God with your questions.
What promise are you still waiting for? Tell me below. Next: Sarai's plan, and a slave girl alone in the desert, whom God sees. Subscribe.
